title: The Tribes East of the Jordan
overview: This chapter lists the families of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, the tribes who lived east of the Jordan River, and tells of their victories and their eventual exile to Assyria.

parts.label: Why Reuben lost first place (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Reuben was Jacob's oldest son, but he slept with his father's concubine (a secondary wife), so he lost the oldest son's privileges. Those rights went to Joseph's sons, while leadership came through Judah, the tribe of King David.

parts.label: Reuben's families and land (vv. 4-10)
parts.note: The family line runs down to Beerah, a Reubenite leader taken away by the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser in the 700s BC. As their herds grew, the Reubenites spread east toward the desert and, in King Saul's time, defeated the Hagrites, a desert people, and took over their land.

parts.label: Gad's clans and records (vv. 11-17)
parts.note: Gad lived next to Reuben in Bashan and Gilead, rich grazing country east of the Jordan. These family records were written down under King Jotham of Judah and King Jeroboam II of Israel, not long before Assyria conquered the region.

parts.label: War with the Hagrites (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: The three eastern tribes fought the Hagrites and their allies, and the writer credits the win to their crying out to God and trusting him. The text plainly records many killed, a hundred thousand people captured and huge herds seized, and some scholars think such large figures may be rounded or inflated.

parts.label: Manasseh and the exile (vv. 23-26)
parts.note: The half-tribe of Manasseh spread north to Mount Hermon, but the writer says these tribes turned to local gods, picturing it as unfaithfulness in a marriage, and presents Assyria as God's tool in deporting them to northern Mesopotamia. Translations differ on whether Pul and Tiglath-Pileser are one king or two, though many historians think Pul was another name for Tiglath-Pileser.

think: When a group's fortunes collapse, why do people so often look for the cause in their own past choices, and when does that kind of explanation help or harm?
